summary:
Burundi criminalises same-sex conduct under the penal code adopted in 2009. No source in this inventory identifies a decriminalisation measure, exemption or statutory protection for LGBT people in the country.

US State Department human rights reports covering 2009, 2010, 2012 and 2015 record discrimination against gays and lesbians as a recurring abuse, with arrests and harassment of LGBT people documented under that framework. The 2015 report sets those findings within a year marked by extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention and media shutdowns.

In December 2023 President Évariste Ndayishimiye publicly called for homosexuals to be "stoned", adding that this is what they deserve. Human Rights Watch, reporting on 19 January 2024, stated that the remarks stoke fear among LGBT people and urged the ruling party to renounce persecution.

SOS Médias Burundi reported on 4 January 2024 that LGBTQ Burundians described terror in the aftermath of the speech. The Iteka League, a Burundian LGBTQ rights organisation operating in exile, characterised the remarks as "a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people"; members of two LGBTQ associations, speaking anonymously, described them as "a real license to kill (us)". No domestic LGBT organisation appears in the inventory, and no source records any official response retracting the call.
tangentialFactors:
The criminal framework sits inside a wider crisis of state violence. The 2015 US State Department report documents extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention and shutdowns of media, while the 2012 report documents torture, extrajudicial executions and prolonged pretrial detention. Protection machinery is correspondingly weak: the reports give no instance of authorities acting on anti-LGBT violence, and the leading LGBTQ rights body works from outside the country.

The 2010 report lists discrimination against gays and lesbians among the country's common human-rights abuses, alongside security-force killings, torture and harsh prison conditions, which places anti-LGBT treatment within a general pattern of abuse by the security forces rather than an isolated policy.
localsOnly:
The 2009 penal code provisions bind Burundian citizens and residents alike; the State Department reporting describes discrimination against gays and lesbians as an ordinary feature of domestic life rather than a measure directed at visitors.

Residents have no domestic advocacy body identified in the inventory. The Iteka League, the principal Burundian LGBTQ rights organisation, operates in exile, and the two associations that spoke to SOS Médias Burundi did so anonymously, indicating the risk attached to visible organising inside the country.

The presidential remarks of December 2023 were addressed to the domestic audience and were reported within the country, so residents live under both the statutory prohibition and an explicit public call for violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state the penalty the 2009 penal code prescribes for same-sex conduct, and contains no prosecution figures, sentences or case names. Whether the December 2023 remarks were followed by arrests, prosecutions or official directives is not sourced.

No source addresses entry or visa screening, gender-marker or passport rules, access to gender-affirming care, facilities or bathroom law, hate-crime designation, or recognition of partners in Burundi. These remain unresolved rather than absent.

The current reach of the Iteka League inside Burundi is not sourced beyond its stated exile status, and no source records a retraction of the presidential call by the government or the ruling party.
